question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Curl of a Vector Field
question.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+{y}^{2})\,i+y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(0,-1).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,-1)} & =\frac{2(0)(-1)}{{0}^{2}+1}-2(-1) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Curl of a Vector Field
question.problem: Given that $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+(2x+3y)\,j,$ what is the scalar curl of $F?$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =2-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that we're given a Frobenius matrix:

- all entries on the main diagonal are ones

- the matrix has only one column (the $2$nd column) where some entries below the main diagonal are not zeros

- all the other entries outside the main diagonal are zeros

To find the inverse of a Frobenius matrix, we simply take the non-zero entries outside the main diagonal with opposite signs. 

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Find the inverse of the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
The given matrix can be obtained from the identity matrix by permuting its columns. Therefore, $A$ is a permutation matrix.

The inverse of a permutation matrix can be found as follows: 

$$
{P}^{-1}={P}^{T}
$$

In our case, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}={[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+2y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & ={e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 2s+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}\cdot 1 \\  & =2s{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}+2{e}^{{s}^{2}+2s} \\  & =2(s+1){e}^{{s}^{2}+2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2s}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2s)+(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s})\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡2s \\  & =-2-2\cdot \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2s}{{sin}^{2}⁡2s} \\  & =-2-2{cot}^{2}⁡2s \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{x+{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x+2{x}^{2}}{x+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{x(1+2x)}{x(1+x)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{2})+\frac{1+2x}{1+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14109012/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2s\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4t\operatorname{sin}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡s.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}
$$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot (-1)+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Vector Field of a Function
question.problem: Find the gradient vector field of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y).$
question.worked_solution:
The gradient vector field of a function $f$ is given by $∇f.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4y)) \\  & =\frac{2}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient vector field of $f(x,y)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2y}\,i+\frac{2}{x+2y}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$
